title: Weak US Jobs Report Pushes October Fed Rate Hike Odds Below 25%
excerpt: Just 29,000 jobs added in September against 90,000 expected, with steep downward revisions — futures markets now see the Fed standing pat at its October 27-28 meeting.
body:
• US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, roughly a third of the 90,000 economists expected, and the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on October 2.
  • The prior two months were revised down by a combined 60,000 jobs — July flipped to a net loss of 10,000 — signalling the slowdown is broader than one soft month.
  • The Federal Reserve meets October 27-28. Futures markets now price less than a one-in-five chance of a rate hike, down from more than one-in-four before the data.
  • For investors: the 10-year Treasury yield eased to 5.18% after touching a two-decade high, and the Nasdaq hit a record — but December hike bets near 90% mean the easing may not last.

The Federal Reserve got more reason to wait before raising interest rates again on Friday, as government data showed the American labor market cooling far more than expected. US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, the Labor Department reported — less than the 90,000 economists had forecast — while the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% from 4.1%.

The details were worse than the headline. August payroll gains were revised downward, and combined with a July revision that flipped the month to a net loss of 10,000 jobs, the two prior months came in 60,000 lower than previously reported. September's gain followed an average monthly increase of just 45,000 over the prior 12 months — a labor market that is barely growing at all.

Where the jobs are — and aren't

Health care added 17,000 jobs, below its recent average of 33,000. Construction added 11,000 and manufacturing 9,000. Financial activities shed 7,000 jobs in the month and are down 129,000 since a recent peak in May 2025. The Black unemployment rate rose to 7.0%; rates for other major groups showed little change.

Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel called the September numbers a "clear miss," but said they mostly extend trends that have defined the market in recent years: "Layoffs haven't picked up, and jobless claims have been falling, so the low hire, low fire market is likely to stay entrenched as we head into 2027."

"Layoffs haven't picked up, and jobless claims have been falling, so the low hire, low fire market is likely to stay entrenched."

— Jake Krimmel, senior economist, Realtor.com

What it means for the Fed

The data lands just weeks after the Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point on September 16 to a 3.75%-4.00% range — its first increase since 2023, in a unanimous 12-0 vote. Most officials who backed that hike also penciled in another before year's end.

But the September jobs report plus cooler-than-expected inflation data have sharply reduced market expectations for the October 27-28 meeting. Interest-rate futures are priced for less than a one-in-five chance of a hike this month, according to CME FedWatch — down from more than one-in-four before the data. A December hike, however, is still priced at nearly 90% probability. Goldman Sachs Asset Management's Lindsay Rosner told CNBC the soft report effectively removes the possibility of an October hike, with December remaining the base case.

Bond markets moved fast. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield dropped to 5.18% on Friday after touching 5.342% a day earlier — its highest level in more than two decades. The 2-year yield, most sensitive to Fed policy, fell to 4.73%. US stocks closed higher, with the Nasdaq Composite reaching a record as investors read weaker employment as a green light against further tightening — particularly welcome for long-duration technology shares whose valuations are most sensitive to rate expectations.

Diaspora angle

For NRI portfolios, the tension matters more than the headline: a Fed on hold in October but likely hiking in December keeps mortgage rates elevated — the 30-year still sits at 5.57% — while supporting rate-sensitive US equities in the near term. A weaker labor market alongside persistent inflation is also the backdrop against which the rupee and remittance flows get repriced, so the December meeting, not October's, is the one to watch.

What's next

The October 14 CPI report is the first test of whether inflation's decline is holding. Then comes the October 27-28 FOMC decision, where anything other than a hold would now be a genuine surprise. The real decision point is December: if labor keeps cooling while inflation lingers, the Fed faces the uncomfortable choice between fighting prices and protecting jobs.
